scenes.narration: Welcome to module one of Toast one oh one, the science of brown. Put a slice of bread in the toaster for thirty seconds and it comes out warm but pale. Leave it for a few minutes and it comes out golden, nutty, and crisp. Nothing was added to it. So in this module, we'll find out what the bread did to itself.

visual.title: The Science of Brown
visual.subtitle: Why toast turns golden, and why it waits

scenes.narration: Most of that change is the Maillard reaction. Amino acids from the bread's proteins react with sugars from its starch. Each reaction makes new flavor and aroma compounds, and brown pigments too. It speeds up a lot once the surface passes about one hundred and forty degrees Celsius. Below that, the ingredients are all there, but they barely react.

bullets.cue: Amino acids from the bread's proteins

scenes.narration: But toast can't brown right away. Bread is roughly a third water, and water can't get hotter than one hundred degrees at normal pressure. So first, the surface has to dry out. Only then can it heat past one hundred and forty degrees, and only then does it brown. That's also why toast is crisp outside and soft inside.

visual.kicker: First it dries, then it browns

scenes.narration: Quick check. On the same toaster setting, which browns faster: plain white bread, or brioche? Pause and decide. The answer is brioche. It has more sugar, so caramelization joins the Maillard reaction and the slice darkens faster.

To sum up. Toast turns brown mostly because of the Maillard reaction. It needs a dry surface above about one hundred and forty degrees. And sugary breads brown faster, because caramelization helps. Next module, we'll pick the right bread for the job.
